questions.question: 43.5% of this IPO's money is an offer for sale. Where does that part of the money go?

choices.text: Into the company, to build new factories.
To the existing owners who are selling their shares.

questions.explanation: In an offer for sale, existing owners sell shares they already hold, so the money goes to them. Only the fresh issue, ₹2,830 crore here, reaches Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses Limited.

numbers.name: ofs_share
numbers.label: Share of the IPO money going to sellers

questions.question: Sales went from ₹12,364.37 crore in FY24 to ₹15,913.32 crore in FY26, which is 13.4% a year. How would you describe that?
questions.explanation: 13.4% a year is slow growth: Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses Limited is growing, but not by much.

questions.question: Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses Limited owes 0.47 rupees of loans for every rupee of its owners' money. Which is closest to the truth?

choices.text: Its loans are small to manageable next to what the owners have put in.
Its loans are heavy: lenders have more riding on it than its owners.
Loans never matter for a company that makes a profit.

questions.explanation: At 0.47 rupees of loans per rupee of owners' money, Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses Limited's owners have more in the business than its lenders.

numbers.name: debt_to_equity
numbers.label: Loans for every rupee of owners' money

questions.question: An unofficial grey market premium of ₹22 a share is being quoted. How much should you rely on it?

choices.text: Completely: it tells you the listing price.
A little at most: it is unregulated and easy to push around.
It is set by the stock exchange.

questions.explanation: The grey market premium of ₹22 for Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses Limited is gossip with a number on it: nobody regulates it, and it often turns out wrong.
